transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-15
Start time: 08:15 UTC
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Patel (Redwood SRE), Samir Rao (CTO - Aurelius Health), Lina Gomez (Cloud Architect), Jon Park (Security), Meera Iyer (ML Platform)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, we planned a deep dive on the private VPC deployment and how networking choices affect runtime. Diego will drive the runtime stuff, Priya will cover ops/architecture. Samir, Lina, Jon, Meera, thanks for making time.

[00:18] Samir Rao: Yep thanks Maya; we want to make sure when we move to private VPC the latency stays within SLAs and that security and audit are clean. We've had some concerns around PrivateLink vs. NAT and also DNS resolution in our private hosted zones.

[00:30] Diego Alvarez: Great, so agenda quick: control plane connectivity (PrivateLink / S3 / control-plane calls), egress for model downloads and telemetry, subnets/AZ layout, DNS and private hosted zones, then runtime impacts — KV cache placement, batching, and quantization tradeoffs.

[00:48] Lina Gomez: Perfect. FYI we run in 3 AZs and prefer no cross-AZ data paths for hot-path inference to avoid egress cost and latency. Our infra team wants explicit NAT constraints — we try to avoid many internet-facing NATs.

[01:05] Priya Patel: Noted. On Redwood side for Private deployments we offer a private control plane option: the control plane reaches your VPC via PrivateLink. Data plane (inference) can run entirely inside your VPC if you deploy the on-prem package or use our VPC connectors for dedicated pools.

[01:25] Jon Park: Quick security Q: does control plane telemetry leave our VPC? We need KMS integration and audit logs retained for 1 year.

[01:33] Maya Chen: Short answer: telemetry and audit logs can be routed to your S3 and CloudWatch equivalents; we support KMS/HSM integration for keys. We'll send the SOC2/KMS runbook after.

[01:44] Diego Alvarez: Ok jumping into control plane options. Option A: AWS PrivateLink to our control plane endpoint — this creates an ENI in your VPC and traffic to the control plane never traverses public internet. Option B: NAT egress to our control plane over TLS — simpler but traverses NAT and outbound path. With PrivateLink you get lower variance in latency and better security posture.

[02:12] Lina Gomez: Is PrivateLink required for model artifacts? We host models in S3; will the runtime pull weights during startup?

[02:20] Diego Alvarez: Good point. The initial model download (weights) typically pulls from our artifact store; we can either mirror the model artifacts into your S3 bucket or allow the runtime to pull through PrivateLink. For large models we recommend mirroring to local S3 to avoid slow pulls on cold starts.

[02:38] Meera Iyer: For our profiles cold-starts are the pain — 2-3 second noticeable lag for model warmup. How much does KV cache locality help? If the KV cache gets hit, do we still need cross-subnet calls?

[02:49] Diego Alvarez: KV cache (we sometimes see it transcribed as K-V cache in notes) is per-runtime instance; if you colocate clients and instances in the same subnet/AZ, KV cache hits avoid network calls entirely because the cache is in-memory on the GPU host. When you use multi-node sharding where requests route across nodes you will see cross-node traffic — we recommend an affinity policy to keep session affinity in the same AZ to preserve cache locality.

[03:20] Lina Gomez: So subnet layout matters — keep GPU pools and API gateways in same AZ, got it.

[03:31] Priya Patel: Also batching behavior: we do continuous batching at the runtime; latency SLOs depend on batch size and queueing. If your traffic is mostly intra-AZ and low variance, batching will be efficient. Cross-AZ variability can increase tail latency because packets may arrive slower from certain AZs.

[03:52] Samir Rao: What about quantization? If we quantize models to int8, any special networking effects?

[03:59] Diego Alvarez: Quantization mostly affects memory footprint and per-token CPU/GPU computation. Network impact is negligible after the model is loaded. However, smaller models reduce cold-start time so they indirectly reduce network penalty due to fewer artifact downloads and quicker cache warmups.

[04:20] Jon Park: DNS — we use private hosted zones and split-horizon. Will Redwood endpoints be resolvable inside our VPC?

[04:28] Maya Chen: Yes, we support private DNS configuration. For PrivateLink we recommend creating private hosted zones and mapping the control-plane domain to the VPC endpoint. We can provide a terraform snippet. Diego, do you have the snippet link?

[04:40] Diego Alvarez: I do, will include in follow-up. Note: if you use PrivateLink, make sure your resolver rules are set so that control plane domain resolves to the VPC endpoint. Otherwise traffic may try to exit via NAT.

[04:56] Lina Gomez: About NAT: we have strict rules limiting outbound connections and only a couple NAT gateways. Does Redwood need lots of egress?

[05:05] Priya Patel: For runtime operation: after initial model pulls, normal inference calls remain within VPC when using our Private deployment. The control plane calls are lightweight (heartbeats, metrics), so egress bandwidth is low. If you choose NAT-only control plane, you'll see periodic TLS connections to our endpoints — measured in KBs per minute, not GBs. The main egress would be model downloads and large eval dataset uploads.

[05:30] Meera Iyer: Good. For the pilot we will mirror models into our S3; that avoids big egress hits.

[05:38] Diego Alvarez: On affinity and routing: we can configure node affinity policies to prefer same-AZ routing and local KV cache hits. That is a runtime config parameter. We also have a fallback policy that can route to a different AZ if capacity is constrained, but you can set strict affinity for latency-critical workloads.

[05:58] Samir Rao: If strict affinity causes capacity issues, what's the graceful degradation? Does it queue or failover?

[06:05] Diego Alvarez: We support two behaviors: queue-with-timeout (wait for local resource with bounded latency) or immediate-fallback to cross-AZ node; you pick based on SLOs. For e.g., healthcare triage we usually recommend immediate-fallback with a slightly cheaper model variant as a fallback, that keeps throughput while lowering per-token cost.

[06:30] Lina Gomez: Can you explain the PrivateLink setup topologically? I want to ensure it's congruent with our transit gateway.

[06:39] Priya Patel: Sure — PrivateLink creates an endpoint service on Redwood's side and a VPC endpoint in your VPC. That VPC endpoint projects as an ENI in the chosen subnets. If you're using a TGW, you can route to that ENI via route tables. Be mindful of security groups on the endpoint interface.

[06:58] Jon Park: Are there port requirements? We run very tight SGs.

[07:03] Diego Alvarez: Control plane uses HTTPS (443) primarily. For model artifact mirroring we read/write to S3 using standard S3 endpoints — no extra ports. If telemetry goes to your internal collection endpoints, we can use HTTPS as well.

[07:18] Meera Iyer: On benchmarking — we want to run a pilot simulating 10k qps mixed short/long contexts. Any recommended config for batching and KV sizes?

[07:28] Diego Alvarez: For mixed workloads, we recommend an adaptive batching config: max batch size to 64 for short requests, 16 for long-context requests, with latency cap of 200ms for P95. KV cache size depends on session lengths; we typically allocate enough KV to hold last 2-4 sequences per session. We'll share a spreadsheet with sample heuristics.

[07:50] Samir Rao: Sounds good. Can you also outline failure modes for PrivateLink? What happens if the endpoint becomes unhealthy?

[07:58] Priya Patel: If a PrivateLink endpoint fails, traffic will not automatically shift to NAT. You should design route tables and fallback policies. We can help configure policies so the control plane fails over to a fallback public endpoint via your egress if you choose. We also support multi-region endpoints to improve availability.

[08:18] Lina Gomez: On routing and VPC peering or TGW, we often prefer TGW. Any gotchas with TGW and PrivateLink?

[08:26] Diego Alvarez: TGW works; ensure that TGW route propagation reaches the subnets where the VPC endpoint ENIs live. Also note that PrivateLink ENIs are regional; if you're peering across accounts, permissions need to be set; we'll include the terraform snippet.

[08:40] Jon Park: A couple security asks: 1) KMS integration for model encryption in transit and at rest, 2) audit logs to our S3 with object-level logging, 3) proof of SOC2 controls.

[08:51] Maya Chen: We support customer-managed KMS keys and integrate with HSM for critical workloads. We'll attach the SOC2 pack and KMS integration guide in the follow-up.

[09:01] Meera Iyer: Any notes on throughput per GPU and network NICs? We have NVLink-backed instances and sometimes the NIC becomes a bottleneck for cross-node KV sync.

[09:10] Diego Alvarez: Good question. For large-scale sharded setups, network can dominate if KV sync or model parallel ops cross nodes. For inference-only (sharded by session) we prefer single-host KV locality — then NIC isn't stressed. If you plan very wide model parallelism, choose instances with 100Gbps NICs and consider colocating sharded groups in same AZ with EC2 placement groups to reduce network hop.

[09:38] Lina Gomez: So for our initial pilot we'll keep single-host KV locality and strict AZ affinity, mirror models to S3, use PrivateLink for control plane, and allow fallback to NAT in case of endpoint issue. That sound right?

[09:50] Diego Alvarez: Yep. We'll provide recommended Terraform, a checklist for VPC endpoints, SG rules, and a sample runtime config for affinity and batching.

[10:00] Maya Chen: Let's recap next steps: Diego to share benchmark spreadsheet and runbook; Priya to share terraform snippets and PrivateLink checklist; Lina to send subnet plan; Jon to confirm KMS/audit details. We'll schedule the pilot kickoff for week of 12/21 pending those artifacts.

[10:20] Samir Rao: Sounds good thank you.

[10:25] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the docs and link to the demo cluster for the pilot.

[10:30] (call ends)

Notes about transcript quality: some names and acronyms were auto-trancribed slightly off (e.g., K-V cache, Private Link vs PrivateLink). Links/resources referenced: Redwood Private VPC runbook (shared in follow-up), terraform snippets, benchmarking spreadsheet.
